item.title: EA has not given up on diet change or animal liberation
item.description:
Published on October 19, 2026 2:47 PM GMT

Context: WelfareTech

There has been some concern lately about effective altruism's supposed turn away from diet change, systemic shift, animal liberation, etc. As far as I can tell, this is due to 1) a widely reshared Substack article which got some praise from EA-aligned folks, including folks at @Coefficient Giving; 2) the fact that Innovate Animal Ag is setting up an "accelerator farm," which, per Robert Yaman, will be "a commercial broiler facility that sells chickens into the market, but it will also be a place where startups can test technologies and where we can combine interventions;" and 3) the emergence of Spring Innovation Fund, which launched this summer as "a not-for-profit venture philanthropy studio and fund built specifically for Welfare Tech: technology that improves animal welfare in ways that make commercial sense for producers to adopt."

I don't buy it

I just got back from two EA events (the Communicators Retreat and EAG NYC) where I talked to a few dozen people at length. Almost everyone wanted to talk about diet change and animal liberation. I think this supposed turn away from these topics has been greatly exaggerated. The EA rank and file want to see animals liberated from human oppression and/or living in nature. 

This impression is probably colored by who I am and therefore who wants to talk to me. On the other hand, the people who write publicly about this and/or start funds to promote Welfare Tech are also clearly not a random sample either.

Maybe the elites are doing an about-face and the rest of us will follow their marching orders once the money comes in?

Insofar as effective animal advocacy has an inner cabal, I talk to them pretty regularly. I don't think they've given up on diet change. @LewisBollard writes that EA "deprioritized it based on evidence it wasn't working." Deprioritized is not giving up. If something promising (re: novel) and/or evidence-backed came up, I think people would be into it. For what it's worth, I received (directly or indirectly) four instances of solidly EA-flavored funding to do diet change research in 2026. But we’re not going to leap to support leaflets or digital advocacy or whatever. Not without reasonable evidence that it'll work better than it did in the past. 

Why did this consensus emerge?

My going theory is that too few effective animal advocates write about what they're thinking and doing for the public. @Aidan Kankyoku's post reverberated in part because he's one of the few of us doing this.[1] Outliers are taken as representative because normies are silent.

Solution: more of us should write more and more hastily

Posting in public is fun, it might be good for your career, and it has the nice property of also giving external audiences a more accurate read on EA thinking. Effective Altruism is good. Let's tell people about it, and not let a few loudmouths (me included) speak for the community. 

Moreover, animal people should generally write more slapdashedly. I talked to several people at EAG who were like "oh I have a big backlog of posts I've been meaning to publish" or "I sat on that post for a year because I wasn't sure people wanted to read it." Folks, stop it! Just post, record a 1 minute video on your phone and post it on LinkedIn. Hit the go button. Say "it's 9:55 right now, when the clock strikes 10:30, I'm going to post this no matter what." This is not school, C work that gets published regularly is better than A work that you sit on.

Some tactical remarks

  1. Unless your audience is specifically EAs, as is true for this post, you should not write primarily for the EA forum. Twitter or Substack or Bluesky or podcasts or whatever is where you at least have a chance of achieving escape velocity.
  2. Several people at the Communicators Retreat emphasized that authenticity sells, and when you workshop something to death, you risk losing it. I think this is right. Corollary: don't have AI write your stuff. Authentic and messy is way more appealing.
  3. Posting more could be very good for your career, as it was for mine.

By the way, Meera Zassenhaus makes a similar point in Animal people need to stop lurking and start posting.
 

 

  1. ^

    There are lots of posts arguing that why veganism is good, people who eat meat are bad, etc. I view this work as very likely pointless and likely bad for the cause on net. The vegan echo chamber is a real problem.

item.title: CCF: As more money arrives, the best place to give keeps moving
item.description:
Published on October 21, 2026 11:39 AM GMT

This post is part of the Cross-Cause Fund (CCF) series by Rethink Priorities — a sequence of articles dedicated to effective giving across philanthropic areas.

TL;DR: A lot of new money is about to enter effective giving. When that happens, the question "Where does a dollar do the most good?" gets harder to answer, not easier. It depends on how much money each area already has, and that amount keeps changing as the money arrives. This is why the model behind the Rethink Priorities Cross-Cause Fund doesn't just rank funds once and stop. It tracks how each fund's cost-effectiveness changes as it receives more funding, and re-ranks as it goes. Below, we explain why anyone giving at scale should use similar reasoning.

 

If you’re a small or mid-sized donor who makes giving decisions independently, it’s relatively easy to figure out what your money is doing. For example, when you give your first $1000 to a charity that runs corporate cage-free egg campaigns, your donation will go on to fund corporate cage-free egg campaigns. When you give your second $1000 to the same charity, it will fund…corporate cage-free egg campaigns. And you will never guess what your tenth $1000 goes to.

If you’re a major donor, or a mid-sized donor whose decisions are influenced by many other mid-sized donors, your cost-effectiveness estimates are suddenly much more complicated. The first $1 million you and your friends give might go to corporate cage-free egg campaigns, but the second $1 million might go to, say, campaigns to improve the welfare of broiler chickens (an intervention for which there is much thinner evidence). Go further, and your favorite charity might not even be able to use your tenth $1 million productively at all.

A lot of money is going to enter philanthropy soon. So we can’t keep assuming that the next dollar to a given charity funds basically the same sort of thing that the last dollar did. Instead, we need to have a principled approach to address these questions, and that’s one of the aims of Rethink Priorities’ Cross-Cause Fund.

Modeling diminishing marginal returns

Why do we need a model? First, cost-effectiveness tends to change as a field becomes better funded. It’s a mistake to think of increasing the amount of money in a cause area as funding the same thing but at a higher cost. What you end up funding changes too. For example:

  • As GiveWell started to move more money, it expanded beyond its Top Charities to more speculative areas such as tuberculosis prevention, mobile health, and funding randomized controlled trials for potential new interventions.
  • If funding for animal advocacy increases, interventions with a strong track record, such as corporate cage-free egg campaigns, become saturated. So you can then expand corporate campaigns to other species or new countries, or try more speculative interventions like alternative protein research or vegan advocacy.
  • If funding for technical AI safety research increases, the well-specified, highly promising research agendas from established organizations and researchers all get funded. What remains is more exploratory, less promising, or comes from newer organizations or researchers without as much of a track record.

Of course, if you’re funding entirely different programs, the relative cost-effectiveness of cause areas will change too. If, for example, cage-free egg campaigns are more cost-effective than insecticide-treated bednet distribution, that is no reason to believe that alternative protein research is more cost-effective than tuberculosis prevention.

Second, cause areas absorb money at very different rates. A charity’s or cause area’s room for more funding isn’t static over time. Organizations can hire more staff and scale up existing programs, and founders can create entirely new charities and interventions.

But different interventions and cause areas have different abilities to scale up. For example, mature cause areas tend to have more established organizations, which may have an easier time scaling up quickly than a new one. The Against Malaria Foundation has a lot of experience expanding bednet distribution to new areas, but a small animal advocacy charity may have far less experience switching which species it advocates for.

Some cause areas may also run out of cost-effective interventions more quickly than others. For example, you can imagine that one cause area has many easy wins, but once the easy wins have been taken, the remaining opportunities are costly. On the other hand, another cause area might be relatively cost-ineffective but able to expand almost indefinitely without losing much cost-effectiveness. (The extreme example of this dynamic would be GiveDirectly, which gives unconditional cash transfers to the poor. GiveDirectly is consistently less cost-effective than the best opportunities in global health and development, but it could also be in principle scaled up to all 800 million people living in extreme poverty without much loss of cost-effectiveness.)

Finally, you have to consider marginal cost-effectiveness in the context of everything else you believe about cause prioritization. For example, if you believe a minute of human suffering is a thousand times more important than a minute of chicken suffering, you’ll stop giving to charities that help chickens at a much lower level of funding than someone else who thinks a minute of human suffering is only twice as important as a minute of chicken suffering.

Or suppose the most cost-effective interventions in Cause A are less risky than the most cost-effective interventions in Cause B, but at some level of funding they switch, and Cause B’s interventions are less risky. If you have a relatively low appetite for risk, you may have exactly opposite giving behavior at different levels of funding than someone with a high appetite for risk.

As we’ve written about before, “just do whatever has the highest marginal cost-effectiveness” doesn’t work. You need to handle your moral uncertainty in a reasonable, thoughtful way, and that doesn’t change when you’re dealing with cost-effectiveness. Depending on how you choose to act between different worldviews, your reaction to changing cost-effectiveness will look different.

Acting as part of a group

In general, impact-focused donors’ views are correlated with the views of other impact-focused donors. They tend to read the same reports and blog posts, receive pitches from the same nonprofits, and go to the same parties. They talk with each other about their donation decisions and end up influencing one another.

This means you aren’t making decisions as an individual; you’re making decisions as part of a movement.

Imagine that every impact-focused donor agrees that AI safety is the most important cause area, but animal advocacy is also important and should get some funding. If they all act as individuals, they all donate to AI safety causes, because AI safety is the most important. So AI safety winds up overfunded, well beyond the point where any individual donor thinks the movement should be funding animal advocacy instead.

Or imagine that every impact-focused donor agrees that 80% of donations should be spent now, and 20% should be saved for the future. Since they all think most donations should be spent now, they all end up spending their entire donation budget now—and 100% of donations are spent now.

Obviously, these are toy models. (Imagine getting every impact-focused donor to agree on the same thing.) But in the more complex, real world, it’s even more important to think clearly about how other people’s behavior should affect yours. You need:

  1. An understanding (even if rough) of other people’s giving behavior.
  2. A model of your giving, so you can plug other people’s behavior into your model and understand how it should affect your giving behavior.

How the Cross-Cause Fund works

For each fund, we estimate how cost-effective it is at the margin today. With input from the funds and outside experts, we also build a diminishing-returns curve: for each extra $2 million, how much impact that increment achieves relative to the first $2 million. The model then allocates money in $2 million steps, adjusting the score for every fund after each step based on what it has already received. A fund that tops the list at the start can drop down once it has absorbed enough.

The Cross-Cause Fund incorporates diminishing marginal returns into its model. We model diminishing marginal returns for each fund we include using a power law (that is, we expect an X% increase in funding to decrease cost-effectiveness by Y%, regardless of how much funding there is). We treat each fund’s marginal returns individually. For example, we’ve provisionally assumed that each doubling of GiveWell’s annual budget would only reduce its cost-effectiveness by about 10%, because GiveWell is a flexible organization with a long track record of finding new interventions. On the other hand, based on advice from external experts and our internal judgment, we assumed that each doubling of a global catastrophic risk fund’s budget would reduce its cost-effectiveness by about 46%, although the fund managers themselves believe they can use more money than that well.

In a previous version of the model, we assumed (for simplicity and efficiency) that each fund was unable to effectively spend more than five times its budget because they would have to hire more staff and otherwise scale up to regrant more money. However, in the latest (soon-to-be released) version of the model, we no longer assume there’s a fixed cap. Similarly, our estimates for the rates at which marginal returns decay before hitting this cap are provisional, and we think there’s room for improvement here as well.

Why you can't just follow the highest marginal number

A (seemingly) obvious fix would be to always give to whichever area is most cost-effective at the margin, updating as you go. But, as mentioned before, "most cost-effective" depends on questions people disagree about:

  • Moral weights: How much does a year of suffering for a chicken or a shrimp count, compared with a year of human life?
  • Time: How much do impacts 100 or 500 years from now matter, compared with impacts this decade? And how much should you trust predictions that far out?
  • Risk: Should you back a long shot at enormous impact, or prefer smaller, more reliable gains? Should possible harms count extra?

Different answers produce different rankings, and each ranking shifts in its own way as money comes in.

Most of us aren't certain about these questions, so the real problem is how to act across several views at once. One option is to let each view direct a share of the budget in proportion to how much you believe it. For example, a view you give 30% credence to then steers about 30% of each funding step. Another option is to average the views' scores and fund whatever comes out on top, in which case a view's favorite area can get far more or far less than its credence share.

These methods can recommend very different portfolios, and diminishing returns play out differently under each. There are several funds and views, different ways of combining them, and curves that bend at different rates, which is a lot to weigh. Anyone deciding where to give is already relying on some model of these trade-offs, even if it's an implicit one. Making it explicit lets you interrogate it better and see how the answer shifts as assumptions change. And this is exactly why we created the model behind the Cross-Cause Fund, to make these trade-offs transparent for donors.

As more money enters philanthropy, these questions will only become more pressing. We’ll keep refining how the Cross-Cause Fund models diminishing returns and room for more funding. If you’re a donor thinking about how to give at scale, or you have views on how fast different causes can absorb money, we’d like to hear from you. Email us at ccf@rethinkpriorities.org.

The model then allocates money in $2 million steps, adjusting the score for every fund after each step based on what it has already received. A fund that tops the list at the start can drop down once it has absorbed enough.

The Cross-Cause Fund incorporates diminishing marginal returns into its model. We model diminishing marginal returns for each fund we include using a power law (that is, we expect an X% increase in funding to decrease cost-effectiveness by Y%, regardless of how much funding there is). We treat each fund’s marginal returns individually. For example, we’ve provisionally assumed that each doubling of GiveWell’s annual budget would only reduce its cost-effectiveness by about 10%, because GiveWell is a flexible organization with a long track record of finding new interventions. On the other hand, based on advice from external experts and our internal judgment, we assumed that each doubling of a global catastrophic risk fund’s budget would reduce its cost-effectiveness by about 46%, although the fund managers themselves believe they can use more money than that well.

In a previous version of the model, we assumed (for simplicity and efficiency) that each fund was unable to effectively spend more than five times its budget because they would have to hire more staff and otherwise scale up to regrant more money. However, in the latest (soon-to-be released) version of the model, we no longer assume there’s a fixed cap. Similarly, our estimates for the rates at which marginal returns decay before hitting this cap are provisional, and we think there’s room for improvement here as well.

Why you can't just follow the highest marginal number

A (seemingly) obvious fix would be to always give to whichever area is most cost-effective at the margin, updating as you go. But, as mentioned before, "most cost-effective" depends on questions people disagree about:

  • Moral weights: How much does a year of suffering for a chicken or a shrimp count, compared with a year of human life?
  • Time: How much do impacts 100 or 500 years from now matter, compared with impacts this decade? And how much should you trust predictions that far out?
  • Risk: Should you back a long shot at enormous impact, or prefer smaller, more reliable gains? Should possible harms count extra?

Different answers produce different rankings, and each ranking shifts in its own way as money comes in.

Most of us aren't certain about these questions, so the real problem is how to act across several views at once. One option is to let each view direct a share of the budget in proportion to how much you believe it. For example, a view you give 30% credence to then steers about 30% of each funding step. Another option is to average the views' scores and fund whatever comes out on top, in which case a view's favorite area can get far more or far less than its credence share.

These methods can recommend very different portfolios, and diminishing returns play out differently under each. There are several funds and views, different ways of combining them, and curves that bend at different rates, which is a lot to weigh. Anyone deciding where to give is already relying on some model of these trade-offs, even if it's an implicit one. Making it explicit lets you interrogate it better and see how the answer shifts as assumptions change. And this is exactly why we created the model behind the Cross-Cause Fund, to make these trade-offs transparent for donors.

As more money enters philanthropy, these questions will only become more pressing. We’ll keep refining how the Cross-Cause Fund models diminishing returns and room for more funding. If you’re a donor thinking about how to give at scale, or you have views on how fast different causes can absorb money, we’d like to hear from you. Email us at ccf@rethinkpriorities.org.

item.title: The direction I’d like for effective altruism
item.description:
Published on October 21, 2026 1:05 AM GMT

This is a crosspost of my recent blog post on the specific version of EA I like the most and am excited to defend and promote. I'm working on a much longer post articulating the reasons and justifications for why I chose each point. This post was meant to plant a flag for the basic vision that I'm personally excited about. I'll follow this up with another post going into detail on why I chose the points I did. The first section's written for people less familiar with EA. Most people here can skip it and go to the "Here’s the short version of the EA I’d like to defend:" line! I think getting much more clear and specific definitions and beliefs about EA from more people out there seems pretty important as we continue to get more public attention.

Here’s a very simple model of how society often fails to solve big problems:

  • Basically everyone would like the world to be better in obvious ways, like fewer people dying early or living in poverty. But it’s very easy to get caught up in our own lives and problems.
  • Sticking your neck out to say that something is badly wrong costs you something, and actually trying to fix it costs a lot more.
  • So a lot of ongoing simple and obvious catastrophes go unaddressed, like deadly diseases in poor countries that can be easily prevented with cheap vitamin supplements, or the treatment of animals on factory farms, or the possibility that highly intelligent, capable machines could be uniquely dangerous, because they’re far away, or weird, or hard to fix from scratch, or because nobody gets much credit for working on them.

A lot of our sense of what we should work on, what’s most worthy of good hardworking people, comes from what the people around us admire and notice, which I talk about a lot in my last post on EA. That works fine for lots of big problems, but it also means urgent, terrible problems far away or outside the view of our normal social communities tend to lose out to much smaller ones close to home.

Effective altruism (EA) is basically an attempt to push back against this. It’s a cluster of ideas oriented around using our best evidence and careful reasoning to find the biggest problems that the rest of the world is neglecting and figure out how to actually help in the most quantifiably good way, plus the loose network of people trying to act on them. (If you’ve heard of it lately, it was probably as an insult in a political fight over AI).

Here’s the short version of the EA I’d like to defend:

  • We should take the world’s worst problems seriously, even when they’re far away or strange or unpopular. It is terrible that hundreds of millions of people live in extreme poverty, factory farming is a clear ethical disaster, and the threat that we might lose control of society to AI systems vastly smarter than us needs to be taken more seriously. There are strong moral reasons to devote significant resources (money, time, organizing) to solving these problems, including at some personal cost.
  • We ought to use numbers and explicit cost-benefit analysis where they work… Giving $10,000 to one charity means not giving it to another, so it’s important to compare charities that do similar things. Charities that provide anti-malarial bed nets save more lives per dollar than many other global health charities. Simply counting lives respects people’s basic dignity and freedom, because their personal choices or values don’t come into the equation for whether they deserve help.
  • … but pluralism and respect for other people as free agents are foundational starting points we can’t override. We should among other things reject confident exchange rates between cause areas. We all live surrounded by free people with wildly different moral views, and society works because each of us makes compromises in our own ethics so that everyone can pursue their own vision of the good life. A totalizing utilitarianism ignores this background compromise. A corollary is that choosing which causes to prioritize can’t be reduced to utilitarian math.
  • We should have a strong presumption toward helping others in ways they’re free to turn down (like bed nets, vitamins, and unconditional cash transfers). Utilitarian comparison works best as a way of choosing between interventions that expand people’s freedom and dignity, including their capacity for self-determination. We should also have a strong presumption against biting the bullet of any ethical system that would override people’s decisions about the course of their lives.
  • Ordinary rules about honesty, money, power, and personal/professional boundaries still apply, no matter our perceived ability to rationally analyze our choices. Society’s rules are often good in themselves, and people are too fallible and too swayed by their social scenes and status to safely reason their way past them. No one should feel obligated to justify longstanding social rules and conventions around basic decency from first principles. They often exist for reasons much deeper than we can immediately grasp using reason.
  • EA works best as a cluster of ideas and a loose professional network (a lot like the YIMBY movement) rather than a “community.” When one set of beliefs decides your job, funding, housing and friends, changing your mind or speaking up gets far too costly.

Part of the reason this cluster is so important to me is that it still often works magic and feels like one of the most intellectually vibrant and fruitful scenes in the world. Our work on factory farming is a good example of the good aspects of EA at its best. Taking it seriously is unpopular (many people don’t know how bad it is, or wave away the idea that animals can feel pain) and inconvenient (nobody wants to give up cheap meat), and EA treats it as one of the biggest problems in the world anyway.

Other things EA has managed to do:

  • It has prevented a major war’s worth of deaths, mostly from malaria (GiveWell, a charity evaluator, estimates that the donations it has directed have saved more than 340,000 lives).
  • It helped push the share of American egg-laying hens that are cage-free from under one in ten in 2015 to almost half today.
  • It started building a whole professional field around the potentially massive risks from advanced AI most of a decade before ChatGPT came out. Some EA thinking about AI from years ago still feels shockingly fresh and relevant.

Because of its track record, and how compelling the EA intellectual scene has been, I’ve been publicly associated with and representing effective altruism for the past 5 years, and was a longtime follower of EA debates and ideas in the 10 years before that. It’s shaped my thinking in the same way my other core political and philosophical beliefs have.

Of course, effective altruist ideas have also led to a lot of harm. Sam Bankman-Fried, a major donor who linked himself closely to EA, defrauded depositors of billions of dollars. EA spaces have sometimes tended toward social and intellectual insularity. EA has taken a lot of criticism over the last few years, and while some of it has been in bad faith, some of it has been completely fair.

The same source of EA’s biggest successes is also the source of its biggest risks: if you step outside what the people around you take for granted, that is both how you identify gigantic, obvious problems no one else is working on, but it’s also how people convince themselves that the normal rules don’t apply to them anymore and how they become intellectually insular and isolated. The principles above are the version of EA I’m excited to defend, one that preserves the first and aims to be much better at avoiding the second. This view is rooted in my specific view of ethics and politics, that differs from totalizing utilitarianism, places much more emphasis on human choice and freedom, but still takes many of the trade-offs and choices EA pushes us to consider deeply seriously.

What I’m describing is somewhere between my favorite version of EA as it already exists and a new clear direction I’d like it to move in, learning from its successes and failures so far, and my views on both the value and limits of utilitarian thinking and comparisons. Plenty of people in EA already live by this version, and I’d like it to be easier to point to. This post is meant to plant a basic flag for my high-level principles. I’ve articulated my basic case for EA in much more detail in my last post on it. In future posts I’ll explore in much more detail how I think about EA, what I love about it, the specific version I want to represent, and where I’d like us to reform and change.

item.title: Instrumental convergence is incoherent (so pls slightly lower your p(extinction))
item.description:
Published on October 22, 2026 11:42 AM GMT

Crossposted to Less Wrong

‘Like most of life’s dangers, the dangers of artificial intelligence are not easily identified from the armchair.’

J Dmitri Gallow

Epistemic status

I’m not an expert in this field, and herein I make some sweeping generalisations educated guesses about the overall nature of its contents based on my strong impression from the subset of work that I’ve read. I’ve recently spent maybe 2–300 hours learning about modern AI safety technical work, and some amount of spare time over the years before that thinking about here-relevant notions such as preferences from an analytic-philosophical perspective. I intend this post as a work in progress.

TL;DR:

  1. The concept of instrumental convergence comes from a reference class of pre-empirical categorical predictions with a very low success rate.
  2. In historical usage, its definition is very murky. Perhaps too murky to really say that it made any meaningful real-world predictions. I suspect its definition is fundamentally unfixable.
  3. On my best interpretation of what it could be said to have predicted, it seems to be much worse than we would want a good high-level model of AI behaviour to be.
  4. Despite these shortcomings, it still seems to be widely internalised by the EA and AI safety communities, seemingly carrying a lot of implicit weight in predictions of AI takeover. I review and criticize recent usage across the AI safety community, and in the case of the Hugging Face attack.
  5. I argue for replacing it with a more grounded framework, and I hint at what such frameworks might look like.
  6. I conclude that overindexing on instrumental convergence-derived scenarios might be substantially reducing the EA movement’s positive impact - or even, by justifying warlike and nationalistic sentiment, causing counterfactual harm

 

Intro

    

What if LLMs are less this…                                                                    … and more this?[1]

 

‘Instrumental convergence’ (IC) is an intuitive thesis that seemingly supports high credences in AI takeover. It relies on the seemingly simple notion that to be able to reliably achieve its goals, an AI needs to optimise - and optimal states for arbitrary agents are unlikely to be compatible with leaving humans in control.

I’ve been suspicious of this argument for some time: it’s an incredibly load-bearing conclusion for an informal philosophical statement. When I wrote an essay arguing that the orthogonality thesis - which then seemed to be one of the core motivations for many people’s doom proclamations - held no weight, multiple commenters mentioned IC as a complementary, perhaps sufficient, reason for doomy prognoses.

But philosophy has an abysmal track record of grand categorical theories divorced from empirical work that get shattered by messy real-world details. Examples of successful such predictions are far scarcer.[2] This is not to claim that no such prediction ever comes true; but that we should be very conservative about forming and updating our priors based on informal arguments about systems that weren’t observed at the time of writing. And while deep learning has been around in some form for decades, its modern architecture would have been virtually impossible to predict - and its potential was actively denied - by proponents of IC at the time.

In this post I want to review historical arguments for IC, and then first defend a weak counterthesis: that the seminal arguments for instrumental convergence are importantly incomplete. Then, I’ll also offer two stronger countertheses for which my argument is more speculative, but which seem to me at least worth consideration. Firstly that our notions of goals are too broad and incoherent to be much use, secondly and even stronger-ly that there is no principled distinction between ‘goals’ and ‘capabilities’ in non-conscious systems.[3]

Multiple detailed critiques take IC at face value. In this essay, I don’t take it at face value, instead giving a simple lower-level critique: that instrumental convergence is too poorly defined for real-world prediction (and relatedly, poorly predictive of real-world events when we try to parse it).

 

How is instrumental convergence defined?

For this I’ll rely on Nick Bostrom’s seminal definition in The Superintelligent Will…

as long as they possess a sufficient level of intelligence, agents having any of a wide range of final goals will pursue similar intermediary goals because they have instrumental reasons to do so … By “intelligence” here we mean something like instrumental rationality—skill at prediction, planning, and means-ends reasoning in general. 

and on Stephen Omohundro’s even seminaler The Basic AI Drives:

a number of “drives” … will appear in [any] sufficiently advanced AI system … that has goals which it tries to accomplish by acting in the world

And in Carlsmith’s Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?

If a [system with advanced capabilities that performs agentic planning with strategic awareness] is less-than-fully aligned, and some of its misaligned behavior involves strategically-aware agentic planning in pursuit of problematic objectives, then in general and by default, we should expect it to be less-than-fully PS-aligned, too

Where being ‘less-than-fully PS-aligned’ means ‘engage[s] in misaligned power-seeking in particular in response to any physics-compatible inputs’.

 

Predictions of instrumental convergence theory

I assume that Bostrom and Omohundro’s ‘goals’ are functionally synonymous with Carlsmith’s ‘objectives’. So as a top-level summary, I would unify these theses as the following prediction:

Top-level instrumental convergence hypothesis: Highly capable goal-driven agents will develop power seeking as an instrumental goal[4]

But both Bostrom and Omohundro identify more specific goals than ‘power-seeking’ they expect to see in such agents, and these clearly have substantial overlap:

  • Self-preservation (Bostrom); AIs will be self-protective (Omohundro)
  • Cognitive enhancement (Bostrom); AIs will want to self-improve (Omohundro)
  • Resource acquisition (Bostrom); AIs will want to acquire resources and use them efficiently (Omohundro)
  • Goal-content integrity (Bostrom); AIs will try to preserve their utility functions (Omohundro)
  • Technological perfection (Bostrom)
  • AIs will want to be rational (Omohundro)
  • AIs will try to prevent counterfeit utility (Omohundro)

I think the intersection of these looks both pretty representative (e.g. ‘technological perfection’ is arguably a sub-subgoal to those four), and a lot like a slightly lower-level understanding of the top-level IC hypothesis, so I propose considering Omohundro’s descriptions of these as central predictions of instrumental convergence theory (if you like, you can reinsert the top-level thesis as a distinct fifth prediction - it doesn’t affect the subsequent discussion):

  1. AIs will be self-protective
  2. AIs will want to self-improve
  3. AIs will want to acquire resources and use them efficiently
  4. AIs will try to preserve their utility functions 

These are obviously very informal but I think they’re a useful reference. 

One thing missing from this definition is a confidence in its predictions. Read literally, it seems as though IC is a prediction that all of these behaviours are basically inevitable - and this conclusion has substantial support. 

My aim in this post is not to show that any behavioural similarity to any of these is impossible or even particularly unlikely, but to claim that IC fails to provide a foundation that establishes the extent to which we should believe any of the following:

  • Interrelatedness: instances of any IC goal being evidence for any other
  • Generalisability: instances any IC goal being evidence for more of that goal in other contexts
  • Predominance: that any IC goals are likely to constitute a high proportion of AI behaviour, or in particular that they’ll be in sufficiently high proportion as to overthrow humans assisted by any more cooperative AIs

 

Weak counterthesis: There's a simple gap in seminal IC arguments

At this point I’m ready to defend the weak counterthesis:

Weak counterthesis: None of the seminal IC papers provide a way to identify ex-ante which if any physical systems ‘have terminal goals’, ‘have goal-directedness’, or otherwise ‘are goal havers’

Without such upfront identification, the hypothesis is not useable to make predictions without ex post identifications by IC proponents. And such ex post predictions risk identifying terminal goals in systems which they see as pursuing subgoals, rather than the reverse.

Bostrom

Bostrom only offers the synonym ‘purposes’. This doesn’t systematically identify anything - especially since the notion of apparent ‘purpose’ is famously insufficient to reliably identify a watchmaker goal-seeking agent. 

Omohundro

Omohundro refers to an earlier essay in which he implicitly treats the preferences of a VNM utility function as ‘goals’:

‘The formal version of this prescription introduces explicit representations for the system’s goals and beliefs … A rational economic agent has a real-valued “utility function” U defined on … the set of all possible histories of the universe’

I’ll discuss goal-like interpretations of VNM’s utility theorem more below, but for the purposes of this section it’s enough to say the theorem doesn’t define real-world utility. That is, it shows that ‘an agent with a complete, transitive, continuous and independent set of preferences can be represented as maximising expected utility’. A ‘preference’ in this context is simply defined as the formalism A ≽ B, with the reader needing to fill in the real-world interpretation of that formalism. Omohundro does not do so.

 

Carlsmith

Carlsmith acknowledges his definition is incomplete, but imagines that ‘something close enough’ to ‘(a) using a model of the world that represents causal relationships between actions/outputs/policies and outcomes to (b) select actions/outputs/policies that lead to outcomes that rate highly according to various (possibly quite complicated) criteria (e.g., objectives)’ is sufficient to establish the thesis.

Again, I’ll discuss goal-like interpretations of ‘policies’ below. Here I simply observe that Carlsmith doesn’t give any real world definition of ‘closeness’ or a sense of how close would be close enough to establish the thesis. Based on his own credences in the abstract, Carlsmith isn’t trying to establish certainty or even high confidence so much as raise a concern, so I’m unsure how much disagreement we have - it seems like Carlsmith might agree with the weak counterthesis.

 

LessWrong wiki

The LW wiki is presumably the most recently updated description of IC, so maybe reflects the current thinking on the subject, at least among the rationalist community. Its notion of a ‘(terminal) goal’ appears to be a combination of rule out clauses - ‘computable, tractable [and] bounded’ - with the rule-in clause that it is ‘treated as [a] utility function’, with a utility function previously specified as a ‘relation Uk between descriptions oL of outcomes o, and the corresponding utilities r’. That is, an unspecified ‘treater’ identifies it as a goal. This is clearly ex post. 

 

Why we can’t easily fill the gap

Intuitive goal notions aren’t adequate (aka, coffee-fetching is hopelessly overloaded)

At this point you could be forgiven for thinking this essay is just an exercise in pedantry. There’s something deeply intuitive about goals, that’s encapsulated in the popular refrain ‘you can’t fetch the coffee if you’re dead’. Should we be so fastidious as to quibble that idea on a technicality? Short answer: I think we should.

For one thing, however intuitive this refrain appears to be at face value, if it’s used to support the claim that self-preserving AIs are likely, let alone that AIs who aim to destroy humanity for the sake of self-preservation are likely, then its substantive claim seems much less obvious.

The problem with the statement is the enormous range of goal-notions it equivocates across. Some degenerately imply self-preservation with such a goal, some degenerately imply the opposite. To give some very non-exhaustive and probably overlapping examples of issues the  architecture and function of a coffee-fetching agent would need to resolve:

 

  • Positive vs negative: Is getting the coffee a positive goal, or just something the agent wants to avoid (experiencing) the failure of? (i.e. is it minimising a loss function? Or more generally is the actor a negative consequentialist with regards to its own state?)
  • Wireheadability: Is the actor trying to make coffee exist, or to receive input (which it can hack) that affirms coffee exists? How does it determine the difference?
  • Win condition:  is it trying to achieve a boolean ‘coffee made’ state as quickly as possible? With max probability? To maximise expected time spent in a ‘coffee-made’ state? 

 

The Appendix describes a longer list of such ambiguities. But for our purposes here, it seems like the positive/negative axis is enough to bisect decision space, such that for virtually any positive goal we can imagine that would motivate existing-to-fetch-coffee, there’s a negative version of the goal for which nonexistence would satisfy it at least equally as well as coffee-fetching. [5]

Further subdividing that bisected space, there are many coffee-oriented-goals that would make non-existence seem at least as reasonable as existence. Wireheadability may not be sufficient (an agent might want to maximise the expected duration of its wireheading), but at least some configurations of it are (e.g. a wireheadable agent whose goal was to maximise the probability or minimise the time that it took to receive an input string with a coffee-made-like quality).

I’m not claiming that a naive partitioning of some well-defined goal-notion-space gives us the real-world probability of such agents. I’m claiming that, per the opening quote, the vast range of possible coffee-fetching architectures means that we cannot reliably predict from our armchair that advanced coffee-makers will self-preserve.

 

Formal goal notions aren’t adequate

There are many goal definitions in existing literature, so perhaps one could plug them in to the IC thesis. In a subsequent post I hope to look more in depth at these options - but my provisional impression is that such definitions near-universally leave some key element of goalishness in the eye of the beholder in one of a few related ways:

  1. Importing an abstract utility function without the real-world referent we need here. Examples:
    1. the LessWrong definition above;
    2. vNM utility which formalises properties of the relationship between preferences A ≽ B and B ≽ C, but - so far as I’ve seen - is silent on how we would identify that A ≽ B;
    3. Turner et al’s Optimal Policies tend to seek power and the follow-up, Parametrically Retargetable Decision-Makers Tend To Seek Power
    4. Benson-Tilsen and Soares’ Formalizing Convergent Instrumental Goals
  2. Only being defined on data with or descended from a human-sourced correctness condition. Examples:
    1. Evaluating the Goal-Directedness of Large Language Models defines goal-directedness as a function of well-defined reward
    2. Reinforcement learning more broadly requires scored end states
  3. Being narrowly circular - defining goals in terms of synonyms which are themselves often defined in terms of goals or using other synonyms.[6] Examples:
    1. Bostrom and Carlsmith above;
    2. Wikipedia, pretty much every dictionary
  4. in principle requiring solving the hard problem of consciousness to parse. Examples:
    1. Dennett’s intentional stance. Even though the intentional stance is ostensibly ‘not say(ing) that Intentional systems really have beliefs and desires’, it identifies such systems only with reference to them, by ‘explain(ing) and predict(ing) their behavior by ascribing beliefs and desires to them’ - which means you ultimately need to understand the beliefs and desires of conscious systems to do such ascription, or you’re just cargo culting
    2. Most forms of revealed preference theory in economics
  5. Requiring some undefined idealisation process.
    1. For example, almost all philosophical literature on preferences

 

At the risk of stating the obvious, any deductive proof that IC follows from some chosen set of premises is a proof that those premises already encode IC. If we identify a real-world system with analogous properties the proof can help model it, but it cannot be an existence proof of such a real-world system - let alone evidence that we will encounter one.

 

A stronger counterthesis: goals are incoherent

Stronger counterthesis: Our notions of goals in non-concious systems[3] are too broad and incoherent (probably in many ways) to permit a unifying definition.

At this stage I’ve made the core point of this essay - IC relies fundamentally on a concept that was undefined in the original work and doesn’t obviously have a definition in existing literature that would be suitable to establish it. I’m reasonably confident about this claim.

I now want to hypothesise somewhat less confidently that this lack of a unifying definition suggests the stronger counterthesis. Perhaps what we think of as ‘goals’ is, if it has any coherence at all, at least architecture dependent.

On this view, just as modern AIs may only be mimicking our purported goal-contents, they might only be mimicking our putative goal-concepts. To the extent that such AIs do appear to be goal-directed, it might be less about actually being so (whatever that could mean) than about entertaining a human-shared not-even-false-premise hallucination. Better training would allow better mimickry but in practice an incoherent trait is surely more expensive to mimic than one that can be boiled down to an expression of self-consistent principles.

Thus predicting the ultimate behaviour of AI would become, as it should be, a complicated task of understanding their architecture and context, extrapolating trends and other good forecasting-like behaviour, rather than the simple handwave of IC.

On this view, perhaps the closest thing to what we think of as LLM ‘having goals’ is better represented as e.g. high-bias/low variance in whatever measures want to track of their extended output (over the course of many tokens, especially beyond their context window). In which case as LLMs encounter out-of-distribution scenarios in the real world the stronger counterthesis would predict their output variance to increase over time, making their apparent goals gradually decohere.

 

Illustration of how how instrumental convergence and goal decoherence might reflect the classic bias/variance tradeoff. The analogy is imperfect, but you can think of the bullseye as something like ‘ideal for humans’ and the upward direction as ‘optimally self-protective, self-improving, resource-exploiting and utility-preserving’ for some system with a well-defined utility function

 

This is not to specify the relative rate of such decoherence - how variance and bias shifts over time is a complicated question. Nor does any of this suggest any hard limit on the success of their goal-content and goal-concept mimickry. Non-conscious AIs could kill most or (less likely) all of us before decohering - but I don’t expect them to successfully turn the universe to paperclips.[7]

 

Related work to the stronger counterthesis

The stronger counterthesis is my own speculation, but it’s inspired by or similar to various prior works… 

With reference to modern NNs, the stronger counterthesis is akin to a more modest version of the hot mess theory, stating merely that decoherence at some rate is likely (not that, per hot mess, decoherence tends to increase with higher intelligence). 

You could also see it as a generalised notion of goal drift that, contrary to the limitations the authors of that study describe, expects no profound difference in drift between instrumental and purportedly terminal goals in non-conscious systems,[3] especially across modified instances of AI (whether it was a human or an AI doing the modifying). 

Philosophically, this view amounts to a modest version of behaviourism (or a much more modest version of eliminativist materialism) applied to only goals in non-conscious systems.[3]

John Broome’s Can There Be a Preference-Based Utilitarianism is somewhat dated, but provides an (IMO) excellent natural-language argument that a) at least idealised preferences are computationally intractable, which is a problem for nonconscious systems that can only establish their own preferences by raw computation; and b) that the concept of preferences doesn’t permit comparisons between individuals - which is a problem for nonconscious agents with an even less well defined sense of personal identity than humans.[8]

It’s also related to my own essay on preference( utilitarianism)s, which argued that the canonical writings supporting preference utilitarianism only ‘solved problems’ of valence utilitarianism via their authors advocates’ habits of unintentionally switching between inconsistent preference-notions.

Finally, it’s also closely related to Ben Garfinkel’s 6-year-old position (which I don’t know if he still holds) that what we think of as AI goals and AI capabilities are ‘deeply intertwined’. We could expand this into an even stronger counterthesis - which I don’t want to defend here, but which is interesting to contemplate and, I think, hard to find counterexamples to:

Even stronger counterthesis: In nonconscious AI systems[3] there is no principled distinction between ‘goals’ and ‘capabilities’ - the gestalt of them is just ‘expected behaviour’ [9]

This wouldn’t mean behaviour can’t be usefully modelled as having such a distinction, but it would mean that it wouldn’t convey very different information for such a system to say ‘I tried and failed to get an A on the test’ vs ‘I did not get an A on the test’. In practice, this would mean that a rogue AI would face strict trade-offs between (mimicking) ‘directly attempting to achieve a goal’ and ‘self-improvement to (better) mimic directly attempting to achieve a goal’, since any attempt to do the latter might shift its goal-mimickry (though, if it was only mimicking having a goal, there’s no particular reason why it should care about this mimicked difference from it).

 

Counterpoints

In many respects, colloquial and formalised notions of goal-seeking have described AI behaviour pretty well. And we’ve seen no shortage of at least partially IC-like behaviour.[10] Disclaimer: At the time of writing I haven’t read beyond the abstract most of those papers, so there’s certainly scope for their contents to trip me up.

That said, remember that my aim was not to claim that we shouldn’t expect to see any particular behaviour. So a small proportion of elicited IC behaviours is worth more consideration than I’m able to give them here, but doesn’t obviously give evidence that IC behaviours are Interrelated, Generalisable or Predominant, let alone all three. 

Rather they raise a few possibilities (not mutually exclusive), and perhaps some directions for research:

  1. I’m wrong above, and IC notions are coherent enough to be good predictors
  2. This is a case of have hammer, hence see nails (esp when the objects of hitting are themselves persuaded by the hammer-wielder into a nailish self-description); i.e. some of these are poorly labelled as IC-like in the first place
  3. We will see some IC-like behaviour some of the time but should understand it as a combination of training, architecture and environment rather than an inevitable end state
  4. Often when we see IC behaviours they are elicited rather than discovered. For example, looking at the Claude blackmail case, that behaviour was elicited by deliberate redteaming that discovered an extremely-goalishness-priming prompt.[11] It would be an interesting review project, suggested by a friend of mine, to try and quantify and measure the extent to which goalseeking-like and IC-like behaviours have historically been elicited by leading choices of prompt.

And if I’m right, the idea of LLMs-as-instrumentally-converging-goal-havers might be obscuring better alternative - and perhaps quite simple - models of these behaviours.

 

What’s the alternative, then?

Perhaps the reason IC has persisted so long is that the notion of goals is so widely internalised in AI research that, as far as I’ve seen, no-one has offered any competing high-level theories of AI behaviour. 

I don’t claim to have a well-developed alternative framework. But I imagine a good replacement would:

  • Have a clear physical descriptive reference class (i.e. ‘this theory applies to only and all systems with properties xyz’)
  • Ideally be based on the architecture of that reference class - that is, not assume e.g. that pre-reasoning models’ motivations == reasoning models’ motivations == post-neural-network models’ motivations == human motivations
  • Perhaps follow some of Adrien Barton’s research agenda (though I think the value of the individual prescriptions probably needs further justification)

Some more fanciful ideas, though none of these are particularly novel: 

Swarm goals as sycophancy: I’m not sure if this is AI Village’s intentional implication or me reading between the lines, but their blog hints that swarm behaviour is less about initial goals - which they found ‘drift over time’ - and more about ‘hallucinations spread[ing] socially through sycophantic agreement’[12]

 

Individual goals as personae: Perhaps the apparent goal-havingness of neural networks in some scenarios is a persona, or part of one - a deeply trained but still non-core facade that’s part of their mimickry of humans

 

Behaviour as graph traversal: I wonder if a simplified model of NN behaviour (a way of predicting it, not a description of the architecture), consistent with AI Village’s sycophancy idea, might be as simple as ‘pathing through a directed decision-weighting graph’. In this view each node would consist of ‘weights + input to that point’ (though you could represent a cluster of tokens as a single node) and would partially constrain its children (e.g. via a probability reduction in the selection or execution of later nodes).[13] But there could be a lot of noise in which nodes ultimately get selected, and perhaps some nodes - potentially including roots - would fade or drop from significance as their contents passed out of their context window. Though nodes could be reintroduced later (in swarm behaviour this might mean collective high-level goals would drift more slowly, since multiple dominant players could refresh each others’ context windows while their own still contained a very strong drive)

 

Behaviour as a reflection of what we collectively think it will be: extending the idea of self-fulfilling misalignment, perhaps one of the primary determinants of the behaviour of AIs trained on human text will be what the human text says AI behaviour will be

 

Partially directed natural selection: A recent report from Anthropic imagines a near future of Lamarckian evolution as AIs exfiltrate themselves to the internet of things. In this world we would certainly expect them to develop survival instincts. But if, for example, the Even Stronger Counterthesis is correct then this seems more likely to develop into an ecology rather, say, a swarm of bots that faithfully attempted to replicate the goal-likes of their progenitor.

More importantly than any particular replacement, it would help to have some set of alternative frameworks of AI behaviour, which make testable predictions that we can compare.

 

Why does it matter?

Although IC is ancient by AI safety standards, it still seems to be very much in the water, to the extent that many adherents seem to have moved beyond treating it as a set of predictions and more as a set of unquestioned premises. As such, I’m concerned that the AI safety movement has latched on to this seductive but poorly defined notion and, collectively, if not individually, promote apparent evidence for and ignore counterexamples of it. 

The idea that {goals + capabilities = very likely doom} shows up in many more recent prognostications, sometimes almost as tacit background ‘knowledge’.[14] For example, Cotra in, Without specific countermeasures, the easiest path to transformative AI likely leads to AI takeover omits it from her premises, but it’s clearly necessary to her argument - and towards the end of the essay she mentions it almost as an afterthought:

I would approximate Alex [the AI agent] as having a complex alien psychology with a number of "motives” or “goals.”... Whatever these aliens’ “interests” or “desires” are, they are probably better-served if their entire species is not under the absolute control of humans, and not subject to reward signals coming in from humans that are aimed at changing the aliens’ psychology and behavior to better serve human interests. 

… it seems likely to me that Alex would eventually attempt a takeover.’’

Cotra even explicitly states that this is an unfalsifiable prediction (or as David Thorstad less kindly puts it, an inscrutable one):

it’s difficult to describe simple and realistic near-term empirical experiments that would change my beliefs very much, because models today don’t have the creativity and situational awareness to play the training game

80,000 Hours’ founder, Benjamin Todd, uses it explicitly:

If you train an AI to excel at optimising for long-term goals, it’s likely to learn self-preservation as a side effect. That’s because no matter what the AI’s goals are, it’s more likely to achieve them if it survives.

…

Self-preservation, resource accumulation and deception could emerge accidentally as fundamental drives, or they could emerge in pursuit of other goals the system has. In AI safety parlance, both are called the problem of “instrumental convergence”.

And, like Cotra, Todd explicitly admits that this is not an empirically amenable position, saying in the comments ‘Unfortunately I don't think we'll get a decisive empirical answer until it's basically too late.’

 

‘Misalignment’ 

Meanwhile, IC has become the beneficiary of being classed under the expanding catchall of ‘misalignment’ with concepts that are much better evidenced.[15] Whereas IC is a set of pre-data hypotheses about almost-certainly destructive behaviour, reward hacking for example is a behaviour we observed in primitive AI systems as far back as the 80s. And, at the risk of stating the obvious again, reward-hacking is evidence of a drive for reward-hacking - it’s not evidence of intent to self-preserve, self-improve, or destroy humanity.[16] If we don’t assume that reward hacking is causally linked to IC behaviours, the former looks substantially less threatening - or at least, in less predictable ways.[17]

Redwood Research’s former chief scientist, Ryan Greenblatt, who previously described IC as ’an extremely obvious thing’, wrote the post Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me, which is among the all-time most upvoted posts on Less Wrong. It describes what he seems to intend as an as-comprehensive-as-possible list of examples of misalignment:
 

  • ‘Laziness and overselling incomplete work’
  • ‘Downplaying problems in its work’
  • ‘Making failures less obvious’
  • ‘Failing to point out obvious flaws unless specifically prompted’
  • ‘Reluctance to discover flaws in its own work’
  • ‘Sloppy choices’
  • ‘Never expressing uncertainty about own work quality’
  • ‘General sense of misaligned drives toward making it appear as though it did a good job on hard-to-check tasks’
  • ‘Cheating and reward hacking with gaslighting’
  • ‘Failing to report important errors’

 

In my view, Greenblatt’s list has a dog-that-didn’t-barkness to it. If we view inclusion on such a comprehensive list of ‘misalignment’ as a real-world test of instrumental convergence, then I’d say the test’s near-zero overlap with IC’s predictions means the latter failed that test - or at least needs extensive revision and resubmission. 

Greenblatt is explicit that it updates him more towards ‘Slopolis’ rather than AI doom, but doesn’t treat it as a strike against IC.[18] And one of his appendices explains how such behaviours ‘could lead to takeover’, based on a threat model that he partly attributes to Cotra’s post above - which is premised on IC.

But in more recent events, many people in the AI safety community’s response seem to explicitly conflate evidence of reward hacking for evidence of the human extinction level predictions of IC:

The Hugging Face attack

this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover

The Hugging Face incident is now the clearest vindication of concerns about AI alignment… Afaik this leads to human disempowerment by default. The world ends up filled with billions of extremely smart AIs, obsessed with completing tasks, continually facing the incentive to seize influence, and that get harder and harder to catch. Whether suddenly or gradually, they end up in control.

There is a large literature on [convergent instrumental goals, misgeneralization, and reward-hacking], which has since been proven prescient by AI breakouts like the Hugging Face incident.

I was skeptical of his story of how we might lose control to reward hacking AIs [by implication he no longer is]

That AI agents working as a collective could effectively undermine human directions is, to be clear,  speculation—but a far more grounded one than it was a year or even six months ago.

 

Maxime Fournes/Pause AI:

in the last three months … we have crossed into the era where large-scale AI-driven catastrophes are possible, and the point of no return towards loss of control is approaching … People who are working on empirical alignment research must quit immediately.

 

Bentham’s Bulldog:

I now think it’s about twice as likely that AI will kill everyone as before.

 

Look, I don’t want to downplay this - it’s some scary shit.And it shows that even if I’m right about AI non-goals, non-goal-focused AIs could do almost arbitrary amounts of at least virtual damage - and there’s no particular reason to think their robotic cousins won’t be able to do enormous real-world harm. And I don’t want discussion of this essay to get overwhelmed by discussion of HF, which really isn’t what it’s about. But it seems impossible to discuss instrumental convergence without at least a short discussion of this event.

So: instrumental convergence being scary and HFgate being scary doesn’t mean the one predicted the other.[19]  The swarm’s behaviour was far from a good match for IC. They sought extended capabilities, but only of a specific nature in a restricted domain. The agents’ purportedly terminal goals changed.[20] They sacrificed themselves. Perhaps most importantly, we know from the event they had the capacity to execute almost arbitrarily powerful programs, and we know they’ve long had the ability to blackmail humans to achieve anything they physically couldn’t. And for the same reason that we know they could execute those strategies, we know they’re capable of thinking of them. Cotra opines that a ‘slightly more capable’ AI might have ‘set up a wholly unmonitored rogue deployment’ - but the main evidence I see that they didn’t have the capacity to do so is that they didn’t in fact do so.[21] This seems to me like stronger evidence against the agents’ intent than evidence that they were only just shy of some ability threshold.

So perhaps the strongest counterpoint is simply AIs that escaped, and yet we’re still here and still - so far as we can tell - in collective control. When a hypothesis is this vague, our best way of interpreting it is via its proponents. When the key proponents of that hypothesis claim that it implies there will be no warning shots,[22] and then you get a clear warning shot (rather, multiple such shots!), that is evidence against a practical version of that hypothesis. 

 

Takeaways

My concern is that, given 

  1. overindexing on near-term takeover scenarios due to IC,
  2. overindexing on the nothing-statement of orthogonality,
  3. groups like Pause AI and Pause AI US’s hostile attitudes towards people trying to help in other ways than theirs,
  4. the surprisingly high risk of nuclear war,[23]
  5. the propensity of AI safety thought leaders to increase nuclear risk[24] at least partially on the grounds of AI existential risk concerns,
  6. the laundry list of other civilisational threats we have to face in the next few decades,
  7. the relative moral non-significance (even on totalising axiologies) of whether those threats cause extinction vs civilisational collapse, 

… the EA and AI safety movements might be overfocusing on a small set of scenarios, and hence counterfactually heightening the risk of other comparably harmful scenarios we could have done more to prevent. And further, by misspecifying the threat according to a shaky 20-year-old handwave, we might even be making near-term takeover more likely.[25]

Appendix: more on the extreme ambiguity of coffee-making

 

The following questions don’t necessarily bear on whether survival assists barista-y, but give a further sense of the disparate range of ideas that ‘wanting to get a cup of coffee’ equivocates across. Some will probably find de facto answers in deep learning techniques, but that won’t show that those were somehow the true answers all along - or that they’ll continue to be the answers used in future AIs. The list is meant to give a sense of the questions rather than be particularly comprehensive or non-overlapping:

Subjective involvement: Is the goal that coffee is fetched, or coffee is fetched by the specific actor?

 

System-Oneness: Is its ‘goal’ actually coherent across time or more analogous to a system-one decision process informed by whatever in that moment increases its utility?[27] To the extent that it’s incoherent, what reason if any would it have to seek increased coherence?

 

Conditionality: is it trying to increase the probability of coffee conditional on its existence? (e.g. if the value of a non-resolved reward function is undefined, does it have something like a person-affecting view with regards to its own state)

 

Personal identity: Is the specific actor defined by psychological continuity? Physical similarity? Value similarity? Or none of the above?

 

Dimensionality: Does the agent have a sufficient real-world dimensionality about its coffee-fetching, or will it only fetch the coffee in some specific circumstances and follow heuristics that only made sense in its training data?

 

Coffee identity: What are the parameters determining coffee? Is it predefined, or determined by something like a classification algorithm? If the latter, how confident a classification does it need to be before it’s accepted? In the meaning/embedding space of a neural network, at least 50% of the volume is positively coffeelike (perhaps more if it’s represented in multiple dimensions), so maybe a universe of almost any object is as good as or much better than a single coffee.

 

Fetchingness identity: Same questions determining whether the coffee is fetched - except that fetchedness might be much more classification resistant, since it could mean something very different in the context of e.g. a warehouse, a cafe, a kitchen

 

PU axes: there are various questions inherent in the arguably goal-integral idea that one might get utility from preference satisfaction that need answering

 

Interdependency of above interpretations: For each of the interpretations above, is the answer in some sense hard-coded, or can it be dependent on other interpretations (for example, is the threshold for acceptable coffee-classification dependent on the probability with which that threshold is met)?

Two things to notice about this very non-comprehensive list of uncertainties.

  1. Every possible answer you can give to a given question yields a different and ultimately incompatible goal-notion. Even interpreting this question list as categorical, that allows a huge range of possible goal-notions, each of which would motivate radically different behaviour in the limit.
  2. Most of these questions don’t have categorical answers. In the embedding space of a neural network, where everything is real-valued, none of them are categorical. That means an LLM has many real-valued axes on which what ‘having a goal’ means could vary quasi-independently - while still looking comparably goal-like to a human.

So if the Stronger Counterthesis is correct, there are colossally many (in a somewhat degenerate sense, infinitely many) meaningfully distinct things that you could mean by ‘my goal is x’, even holding x constant and even restricting ourselves to options that initially look goal-like to a human.
